topic: The Role of Markets and Money
subject: economics

items.title: US tariffs on China were largely absorbed by US importers
items.claim: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019) studied the incidence of 2018 US tariffs on Chinese imports. What did they find?

options.text: Chinese exporters paid the entire tariff
Nearly the full cost of the tariffs was passed through to US importers and consumers; producer prices in China barely changed. The 'tariffs hurt foreigners' framing did not match the price data

items.reveal:
Amiti, Redding and Weinstein analysed customs and price data through 2019. The pass-through was nearly complete to US importers; Chinese export prices for affected goods didn't drop substantially.

Fajgelbaum, Goldberg, Kennedy and Khandelwal (QJE 2020) confirmed the finding using different methods. Subsequent Biden-era tariffs (2024) followed similar patterns. The US-China tariffs reshaped supply chains (Vietnam, Mexico saw substantial increases in exports to the US) more than they raised significant revenue.
items.why: The political rhetoric of tariffs often diverges from the economic incidence. Trade policy effects are empirically measurable; the empirics often don't support the political framing.

items.title: The Phillips curve broke down spectacularly in the 1970s
items.claim: Bill Phillips's 1958 paper documented an inverse relationship between UK unemployment and wage inflation. What happened in the 1970s?

options.text: The relationship held perfectly, vindicating Keynesian demand management
The US and UK experienced 'stagflation' — high inflation AND high unemployment simultaneously, which the simple Phillips curve said was impossible
The relationship inverted entirely; lower unemployment led to deflation
Statistical data became unreliable, so no test was possible

items.reveal:
The 1970s combined oil shocks (1973, 1979), wage-price spirals and weak productivity growth. US inflation reached 13.5% in 1980; unemployment was 7.5%. Both up, together.

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps had argued in the late 1960s that the long-run Phillips curve was vertical at the 'natural rate' of unemployment — once expectations adjusted, only the natural rate was stable. The 1970s vindicated them and supplied the intellectual ammunition for monetarism, Volcker and Thatcher.

Modern expectations-augmented Phillips curves are still used but are far less crisp than the original.
items.why: The Phillips curve example is the cleanest case of a model that worked, then didn't. It's also why mid-20th-century Keynesianism gave way to monetarism, with consequences that still shape macro policy.

items.title: Carbon pricing is the textbook fix for a textbook problem
items.claim: Climate change is often described as the largest market failure ever (Stern Review 2006). What's the standard economic prescription?

options.text: Pigouvian carbon pricing (tax or cap-and-trade) to internalise the social cost of carbon emissions; complementary policies for innovation, transition support and distributional fairness

items.reveal:
Arthur Pigou's 'Economics of Welfare' (1920) introduced taxes to internalise externalities. William Nordhaus's DICE model (1990s onwards) extended welfare economics to climate; he won the 2018 Nobel.

Real-world implementation: EU ETS (2005, world's largest cap-and-trade); UK Carbon Price Floor; Canada's federal carbon tax; California; Korea. Coverage and prices vary widely. As of 2023, ~25% of global emissions had a carbon price; average price below social cost estimates.

Distributional concerns and political economy of carbon pricing have limited adoption despite theoretical consensus.
items.why: Welfare economics provides a clear policy answer to climate change. Implementation is constrained by political economy more than by economic theory.
